author: stretchcloud
text:
Eight search APIs, 4,719 completely ordinary queries, nothing malicious in a single one of them. Every API still returned known-malicious content to at least some of those queries.

That's the finding behind AIR Research Lab's new WebSec Benchmark 2026, the first benchmark measuring the security of the web search APIs that AI agents actually rely on. Firecrawl, Tavily and Perplexity came out on top, which still means seven providers below them did worse, and none of the eight tested risk-free. Most "agent security" conversation is about models, permissions and guardrails, the stuff that matters after the agent already has bad content sitting in its context. Web search is one of the most common ways untrusted material gets into that context in the first place, and almost nobody benchmarks it.

This isn't a hypothetical academics invented to get a paper accepted. There's a real body of research on this exact attack surface right now: BrowseSafe documented prompt injection through abandoned websites agents still crawl, WAInjectBench built a benchmark specifically for detecting injection in web agent traffic, SafeSearch runs automated red-teaming against search-based agents, and a separate "Harness Matters" paper found the agent's own tool harness, not just the model, determines how resilient it is to this kind of attack. The open web has always had malware and lookalike sites. What changed is that a page written with hidden instructions aimed at an AI agent, not a human, is now something you can run into on a completely routine search. Once an agent acts on what it reads, it acts with your credentials and your environment attached.

My take: search API providers are going to start competing on this the way cloud providers compete on compliance certifications, not as a footnote but as a primary purchase criterion for anyone deploying agents against real data. Firecrawl's benchmark position here plus the audited knowledge library it just launched both point the same direction: the bet is that trust becomes the moat once every provider's raw scraping capability starts looking the same.

author: gabbytech01
text:
While new CVEs and breaches keep dropping, here’s a quick look at what’s been recorded so far in 2026.

The “2Shell” family has been one of the biggest stories this year.  

PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 & CVE-2026-109619) was actively exploited, including against Check Point gateways where attackers dropped webshells after gaining access.  

React2Shell, Node2Shell/HTTP2Shell, and others in the same pattern followed unauthenticated RCE in widely used components.

Recent additions to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list include:  
- CVE-2026-76466 (Cisco Expressway – hard-coded credentials)  
- CVE-2026-123890 (VMware vCenter – authentication bypass)  
- CVE-2026-129448 (Apache Roller – deserialization)

On the breach side, we’ve seen incidents involving payment processors, financial platforms, and large customer databases across different regions.

The pattern is familiar: critical flaws in common software get weaponized quickly, and many organizations are still slow to patch or detect the follow-up activity (webshells, persistence, lateral movement).

If you’re running anything exposed to the internet, especially PHP, Node, Java, or common enterprise tools, it’s worth checking your patch status and looking for signs of webshells or unusual processes.

You should also make use of @offshield_ai Offshield AI to check for vulnerabilities in your code and patch them up so you wont get breached. https://t.co/sJe3odcVmJ

Stay sharp.

author: Ghost_Jacker
text:
Below is the summary of major system intrusions, data breaches, cyberattacks, and actively exploited vulnerabilities over the past ~24 hours (as of November 23, 2026), with a focus on Microsoft, Windows, Outlook, cloud, and enterprise systems. Information is compiled from public sources including SecurityWeek, The Hacker News, The Register, Malwarebytes, and CISA advisories.
 * Microsoft Azure API Management Classic Vulnerability Exploited (Impacting Norwegian Energy Firms)
   Microsoft confirmed a critical vulnerability in Azure API Management Classic (non-v2) allowing attackers to access secrets such as named values, client secrets, subscription keys, and management API tokens. Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) reported that the flaw was exploited to target energy companies including Equinor and Skagerak Energi. Microsoft identified the issue on November 18 and automatically applied mitigations the following day, though it advises affected customers to immediately rotate all relevant secrets, audit logs, and investigate for potential lateral movement. The impact is primarily limited to enterprise customers on the Classic tier and could lead to unauthorized access to backend APIs or LLM services.
 * Suspected Breach of FBI National Crime Information Center (NCIC) Database
   The FBI is investigating a suspected intrusion into its NCIC system (first reported by CNN and other outlets on November 20). The NCIC is a critical database shared across U.S. law enforcement agencies, housing millions of records on wanted persons, missing individuals, protection orders, and stolen vehicles. It remains unclear whether attackers exfiltrated or altered data, and the attack vector and timeline have not yet been confirmed. This marks the second publicly reported incident involving FBI systems in recent months. The breach affects U.S. law enforcement operations and potentially sensitive personal data, posing significant risks to law enforcement security.
 * Cisco Expressway Hard-Coded Credentials Vulnerability (CVE-2026-76466) Actively Exploited
   Cisco Expressway (clustered Expressway-C/E deployments) contains a critical vulnerability (CVSS 9.8) enabling unauthenticated remote attackers to gain root privileges and execute arbitrary commands. CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, mandating federal agencies to patch or decommission affected systems by November 23. Active exploitation has been observed, including instances where attackers pivoted into internal networks. The vulnerability impacts edge appliances for enterprise video conferencing and collaboration systems. No official workarounds exist; organizations must upgrade to a patched release (such as X15.5.20).
 * GL.iNet GoodCloud Management Service Vulnerability Exploited to Compromise Routers and KVM Devices
   Attackers exploited a vulnerability in GL.iNet's GoodCloud remote management service to push malware—including reverse shells and backdoors—to certain customer routers and KVM devices. The vendor discovered the attack on November 20, blocked the attack vector, and patched the cloud-side issue, though compromised devices still require a secure firmware installation to fully remediate. Affected hardware includes popular travel routers (such as the GL-MT3000 and GL-MT6000) and RM-series KVMs. The impact primarily affects consumers and small businesses utilizing GoodCloud.
 * Microsoft Outlook Zero-Day Vulnerability (CVE-2026-124194) Remains Flagged as Exploited (Patch Deadline Approaching)

author: AGTPinsights
text:
CISA just flagged a critical Cisco Expressway flaw as actively exploited. Here's what you need to know.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency warned federal agencies that attackers are exploiting a recently patched critical remote code execution flaw in Cisco Expressway. The bug is tracked as CVE-2026-76466 and is listed as use of hard-coded credentials.

CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Nov 20, 2026, in a batch of four flaws that also covers VMware vCenter. Listing means there is evidence of active exploitation in real attacks.

Cisco's PSIRT said it knew of no attacks. CISA says they are live. Security firm F6 found attackers using an AI assistant to get root access, then hunt the network for more credentials.

Key numbers:
- CVE-2026-76466, critical RCE in Cisco Expressway
- Added to CISA's KEV catalog Nov 20, 2026
- 103 Cisco flaws on the KEV list since November 2021
- 7 of those also used by ransomware gangs

The flaw is already patched, so the advice is to check exposure and deploy the update.
